terms.title: Terms and privacy
terms.intro: Kadence is an open source tool for training planning for young cyclists, run by Haij. This is the agreement between you and us when you use the edition we run. If you run the code yourself, only the licence applies.

what.title: What Kadence is
what.body: A tool to plan and follow training for riders, coaches and parents: sessions in a calendar, activities from FIT files and devices, check-ins and a season plan. Recommendations and AI proposals are drafts, not answers, and replace neither a coach nor a doctor.

account.title: Accounts and access
account.body: You get in by applying or being invited. We store your name, your email and your workspace's name, and use them to sign you in and to write to you about the service. Passwords are stored hashed, and you can add a passkey and two-factor. We sell nothing, and we do not send marketing you did not ask for.

yourData.title: Your data
yourData.body: Everything you write in Kadence belongs to you and your team, and a rider's training and check-ins belong to the rider. It can be downloaded as a spreadsheet and JSON in one click and deleted again. We do not look at it unless you ask us for help, and we never pass it on.

ai.title: AI
ai.body: With a language model set up, when a coach asks for a proposal, what it builds on — sessions, load and, if the team has turned it on, check-ins — is sent to the model provider. Who that is, is under Settings → AI and in the list of subprocessors. Without a model everything else works as before.

leaving.title: Leaving
leaving.body: You can delete your workspace immediately, without writing to anyone and without waiting. The export is one click away and readable without Kadence. We keep no copy afterwards beyond the nightly encrypted backups, which roll off after 30 days — on the server and in the EU storage they are copied to.

availability.title: Operation and guarantees
availability.body: Kadence is new, and there is no uptime guarantee. We look after your data with encrypted backups every night, but you should download an export now and then. The service is provided as is, without guarantees beyond what mandatory law requires.

license.title: Licence
license.body: The code is AGPL-3.0. You may use it, change it and run it yourself; if you change it and offer it to others over a network, your changes must be available too. What you write in the tool is not covered by the licence — that is yours.

roles.title: Who may do what
roles.body: Coaches are the workspace's owners and admins: they plan for every rider on the team. A rider sees and writes their own data and nobody else's. A parent sees their own child's training once the rider has confirmed the link, and check-ins only if the rider shares them. The database enforces it, not just the screens.

data.title: Your data
data.body: Everything can be downloaded as a spreadsheet and JSON under Settings → Data. The workspace can be deleted completely, audit trail included.

calendar.title: The calendar
calendar.body: The calendar shows one week at a time. On a computer the days stand side by side, on a phone one below the other. The coach can see the whole team at once and drag a session to another day. On a phone you use "Move" in the session's menu. Races, exams, school, camps, holidays and illness sit in the calendar as small labels. The colours on the sessions show how it went: green is as planned, yellow is a little off, red is not done or far from the plan, and grey is not ridden yet. There is always a word beside the colour.

sessions.title: Sessions and templates
sessions.body: A session is built in steps: warm-up, work, rest and cool-down, each with a length and a target in zones, percent of FTP or threshold heart rate, or by feel. Repeats gather steps that are ridden several times. Once the rider's thresholds are set, the targets read in watts and pulse. Strength sessions have exercises, and a programme has a progression, so sets and reps follow along from session to session. Save a session as a template in the library and it can be given to one rider or the whole team at once.

done.title: Done and RPE
done.body: When the session is done, the rider presses "Done". The minutes are already there from the plan. Then the rider says how hard it was on a scale from 1 to 10 (RPE): 1 is very, very easy, 5 is hard, and 10 is the hardest you can. Think of the whole session. Minutes times RPE gives the session's load, even without a power meter. A wrong press can be undone.

comments.title: Comments
comments.body: Each session has one conversation. The coach and the rider write in it, and the rider's parents can read along. There are no private messages between an adult and a young rider. You can edit and delete your own comments, and a coach can remove a comment.

parents.title: Parents
parents.body: The coach adds a parent and sends a link. The parent sees nothing until the rider has confirmed the link under Settings → Me. The rider also decides whether the parents can see the training, and whether they can see how the rider is doing. From the year the rider turns 18, the rider confirms again as an adult.

season.title: The season plan and DCU
season.body: The season runs from October to September. The plan is filled with DCU's hours for the rider's class (U17, U19 or U23 and the year in it), month by month, with DCU's phases: break and free riding in October, distance in November and December, long base intervals in January and February, short hard intervals around March, and the racing season from April. The coach and the rider can change anything, but DCU's numbers and the deviation always stand beside it. Only hours on the bike count. Kadence's seven zones are Kadence's own; DCU's heart-rate bands are shown beside them for comparison.

load.title: Load: fitness, fatigue and freshness
load.body: Every session gets a load. With a power meter it is worked out from power, otherwise from heart rate, and otherwise from how hard the session felt (RPE from 1 to 10) times the minutes. The last works for every session, strength too. An hour at threshold counts 100, and an easy hour at RPE 3 about 17. Fitness is what the last six weeks have built. Fatigue is what the last week has cost. Freshness is fitness minus fatigue: above zero you are rested, below zero tired, and a little below zero is normal in the middle of a training week.

warnings.title: Warnings
warnings.body: Kadence shows the coach when a week goes past the limits, but does not decide. The warnings are: hours on the bike above or below DCU's range for the week, more than 15 % more hours than the last weeks, a ride longer than DCU's limit (U17 at most 4 hours or 120 km, U19 at most 5 hours or 150 km), strength sessions less than 48 hours apart, too little sleep, pain on ATK's pain ladder, and check-ins in the yellow or red zone. Each warning has a word for how much it matters: "Act now", "Take a look" or "Good to know".

checkin.title: Check-in and wellbeing zones
checkin.body: Every morning the rider answers on sleep, energy, mood, fresh legs, calm and pain, and whether they are ill. The answers give a zone for the day: green, yellow or red. Kadence looks at the pattern over three weeks, not at one bad day. The zones build on Kolding Talent's wellbeing model from Team Danmark's guide for parents: when a rider is in the yellow zone for a while, rider, parent and coach have a talk within 14 days, and in the red zone professionals are involved. The coach sees check-ins; the parents only if the rider shares them. Kadence never diagnoses.

devices.title: Uploads and devices
devices.body: Upload a FIT file from the bike computer, watch or trainer under Today, in the calendar or on the rider's page. Kadence reads the file itself, offline too, and puts the ride on the day's session when it fits. Every ride has its own page with curves, time in zones and best power. Wahoo, Garmin and Polar can be connected under Settings → Devices, so rides come in by themselves, and sessions can be sent to a Wahoo or Garmin. Wahoo and Garmin are US companies, Polar is Finnish, and it is the rider's own choice. A bike session can also be downloaded as .zwo, .erg, .mrc or .fit.

keys.title: Upload keys
keys.body: An upload key lets a program hand rides to Kadence by itself, without you being signed in. Create one under Settings → Devices, give it a name, and copy it right away: it is shown that one time only. The program sends the ride's file to the address shown with the key, with the key in the Authorization field, written as Bearer and then the key. The ride lands on the day's session, exactly as when you upload it yourself. The key can only add rides for you. It cannot read anything, and you or your coach can remove it at any time. Give it only to the program that is to use it.

parentsPage.title: The parents' page
parentsPage.body: Under Parents a parent sees their child's week, the form in words, the next race or exam and, if the child shares it, how things are going. The page also has the parents' guide: Team Danmark's and Kolding Talent's ten themes and nine pieces of advice, written briefly in Kadence's own words with links to the originals.

ai.title: The AI
ai.body: The AI may propose, never decide. It can read a coach's shorthand like "3x10 min Z4 / 5 min rest" into steps (the rules manage most of it without any language model), propose a week for a rider, and write a short summary of who needs attention. Nothing goes in the calendar until a coach presses. It never writes to a rider and never deletes anything. Week proposals and the summary read the riders' data, so they only work if the team has turned on "May the AI read the riders' data" under Settings → Team. Without a language model everything else works as before.

phaseInfo.break: rest for body and mind after the season, then short, easy rides. The winter toward next season's goals is planned.
phaseInfo.distance: form is built mainly by more and more volume. Track, MTB and cross riders also ride some intervals.
phaseInfo.base_intervals: relatively long base intervals begin, while the volume keeps rising month by month.
phaseInfo.peak_intervals: around March come the real peak intervals, short and hard, timed to when the rider wants to peak.
phaseInfo.season: training fits the racing, and the season is ridden to the end.

monthNote.10: Break and free riding. Two weeks of full rest is usually enough, a month if the rider is worn out. Then short rides every other day, and other sports are welcome. Plan the winter.
monthNote.11: The first month with a set volume. No hard intervals yet: build the base that later hard training rests on.
monthNote.12: Volume rises. Light planned intervals may begin, short at first (about 5 min) with long pauses. Harder periods are about 10 % of the volume.
monthNote.1: Relatively long base intervals begin while the volume rises. Intervals at least 10 % of the volume and under about 85 % of maximum heart rate.
monthNote.2: Volume keeps rising, and intervals are about 15–20 %. The most intensive work starts 6–8 weeks before the rider wants to peak.
monthNote.3: Around March, short, hard peak intervals, timed to the wanted peak. A camp in the south may be needed for the hours.
monthNote.4: The season: training fits the rider's racing. At most two peaks a season, each followed by much less volume and low intensity.
monthNote.5: The season: training fits the rider's racing.
monthNote.6: A little less volume: many important races, ending with the national championships.
monthNote.7: A little more volume: the summer holiday leaves room to build for the second half of the season.
monthNote.8: A little less volume late in the season, when riders may be worn out, not least mentally.
monthNote.9: A little less volume, but ride the season to the end: there are many races in September.

guide.title: The parents' guide
guide.body: Ten themes and nine pieces of advice on supporting a child who does a lot of sport, written briefly in Kadence's own words. Read the originals at Team Danmark.
guide.credit: Builds on Team Danmark's and Kolding Talent's guide for parents.
guide.guideLink: The parents' guide at Team Danmark

1.title: Why does your child do sport?
1.body: Talk about it, especially when something changes: a new team, an injury, a long spell without progress. If you each have your own reason, it easily causes friction later.

2.title: Before, during and after the race
2.body: Give calm before, be calm and kind during, and let your child talk to the coach and team first afterwards. Praise the effort whatever the result, and see to food and rest.

3.title: Working with the coach
3.body: Raise worries early and directly, at a good time. Let the coach coach, but keep an eye yourself on whether your child thrives in the environment.

4.title: Motivation
4.body: Rather ask "what did you learn today?" than "who won?". Wanting to get better lasts longer than wanting to win, also when things go against you.

5.title: Goals the child can control
5.body: Process goals, like keeping to the plan or practising a corner, are the foundation. Placings cannot be controlled. Do not share the results on social media.

6.title: You can get better
6.body: Mistakes and feedback are part of the way, not proof that you cannot. Your own way of talking about ability rubs off.

7.title: Feedback that helps
7.body: Compare your child with themselves, not with the others: young people develop at very different paces. Ask whether your child even wants feedback from you; they have a coach.

8.title: An everyday life that fits together
8.body: Make the week's plan together, with school, training, friends and time for nothing. At exams school comes first, at championships the sport. Sleep matters most.

9.title: Wellbeing
9.body: Hard spells are normal, but about three weeks of your child having a hard time should not just pass. Yellow means a talk within 14 days, red means help from professionals. Never train with pain or illness.

10.title: Boarding school and upper secondary
10.body: The transition is hard, and many stop here. Talk openly about the choices, and consider agreeing with the coach to cut back a little the first months.

1.title: You are a role model.
1.body: Your child sees how you behave at races, at training and in the club.

2.title: Support, but let your child stand on their own.
2.body: Help with the practical things, and hand over responsibility bit by bit.

3.title: Be a good part of the club.
3.body: Lend a hand, and respect the coach's work.

4.title: Keep an eye on wellbeing.
4.body: You are the one who can say no on your child's behalf.

5.title: Help the joy along.
5.body: The sport should be fun, in the long run too.

6.title: Find out what drives your child.
6.body: And make it broader than winning.

7.title: Praise the effort and what your child learns.

8.title: Remember everything else the sport gives.
8.body: Friends, belonging and things that are useful at school and in life.

9.title: Ask openly.
9.body: And compare your child with themselves, not with the others.

basics.sleepBody: Young people aged 14–17 need 8–10 hours of sleep. Fixed bedtimes, at weekends too, a cool, dark room and the screen away before bed help most. If your child is tired, check the sleep first.
basics.schoolBody: At exams school comes first, at championships the sport. Put school, exams and camps in the calendar, and the coach can take them into account. A session skipped to be with friends can well be a step in the right direction.

coachGuide.title: Coach guide
coachGuide.intro: Advice for coaches of U17, U19 and U23 riders, gathered from DCU, Team Danmark, DIF, Anti Doping Danmark and the law. In Kadence's own words, with links to the originals.
coachGuide.note: The guide is guidance, not rules. Kadence enforces none of it; you, the rider and the parents decide. With injury and illness, the doctor does.
coachGuide.research: What each source says, how old it is, and where the sources disagree is in Kadence's research note (docs/research/traenermateriale.md).
coachGuide.fromHelp: Advice for coaches of young riders: classes and rules, volume, strength, growth, injury, body and weight, wellbeing and more.

role.title: Your role as a coach of young riders
role.intro: The most important thing a coach of U17–U23 riders does is keep young people in the sport and help them develop. Results come after.

points.1: Development before results. A large Danish study of 7,110 young people aged 12–20 found that coaching focused on development, a say and belonging makes more of them continue the next season. A one-sided focus on results and controlling behaviour makes more of them stop, equally in elite and grassroots sport. The study did not include cycling, but the pattern held across the sports it covered.
points.2: Cycling is a sport of late entry. Physiology and body size matter a great deal, and late developers often catch up with those who were early. Do not judge talent on U17 results alone.
points.3: A healthy talent environment shows, among other things, in a suitable total load, patience, room for the whole person, psychological safety and support when things go wrong.
points.4: DIF's coach pledge puts it briefly: develop your athletes through good, fun and involving experiences, and start from each one of them.

safeguarding.title: Child certificates, boundaries and responsibility
safeguarding.intro: As a coach of young people you carry a special responsibility. The law sets the floor; sport sets a higher bar.

points.1: A child certificate (børneattest) is required by law for coaches with direct and ongoing contact with children under 15. A first-year U17 rider can be 14 until their birthday, so in practice it applies to every U17 coach. The club obtains the certificate.
points.2: DIF recommends a child certificate for everyone who coaches young people under 18, renewed every 2–3 years.
points.3: A sexual relationship with a person under 18 entrusted to you for teaching or upbringing is a crime (Danish Penal Code § 223). Agree in the club on what good physical contact is, and keep changing rooms separate.
points.4: Kadence is built for openness: there are no private messages between adults and young riders. Comments on sessions and rides are read by the coach, the rider and the rider's parents.
points.5: DCU runs courses for coaches: B&U Basistræner, Træner 1 and 2, and Kaptajn Landevej for safe group rides. On group rides, riders may ride two abreast where there is room and it causes no danger or undue inconvenience (Road Traffic Act § 49).

classes.title: The classes and the rules
classes.intro: DCU's classes go by birth year, and each class has its own race limits. Kadence works out the class for you.

points.1: U17 is the calendar year a rider turns 15 and 16, U19 17 and 18, and U23 19 to 22. The season runs from October to September.
points.2: U17 road races are at most {u17Road} km and time trials at most {u17Tt} km, and the gearing may be at most {u17Gear, number} m per pedal revolution.
points.3: U19 men race {u19mMin}–{u19mMax} km and U19 women {u19wMin}–{u19wMax} km, with time trials of at most {u19Tt} km. There is no gear limit in U19, since the UCI dropped the junior limit in 2023. Build up work on big gears gradually in the first year.
points.4: A stage race may last at most {youthStage, plural, one {# day} other {# days}} for U17 and U19 and {u23Stage, plural, one {# day} other {# days}} for U23. To enter the youth national championships, a rider must have ridden at least 3 licensed races.
points.5: The longest training ride is at most {u17LongH, plural, one {# hour} other {# hours}} or {u17LongKm} km for U17 and at most {u19LongH, plural, one {# hour} other {# hours}} or {u19LongKm} km for U19. The longest race is shorter than that, so there is no reason to train longer.

volume.title: Volume and season
volume.intro: Kadence plans from DCU's recommended hours for the rider's class and year and shows a corridor around them.

points.1: Train neither much more nor much less than the recommendations. They are guidance for the coach, not a rule.
points.2: In U17 the most important thing is not to train too much, because too much volume kills motivation. In U19 it is natural to raise the volume 10–15 % a year.
points.3: Avoid big jumps in volume, on training camps too. Build in lighter weeks, because recovery is often what releases the progress.
points.4: Do not stop completely in the winter. October is a break and free riding, and then the build starts again.

strength.title: Strength training
strength.intro: DCU's strength programmes, made by Team Danmark, are in Kadence's library with their progressions.

points.1: From November to mid-March, 2–3 strength sessions a week with at least 48 hours between them are recommended, then 1 a week. U17 and U19 riders should reach at least 30 sessions over the winter.
points.2: Strength training is not dangerous for young people and does not stunt growth. Give free-weight lifts time for technique before the load goes up.
points.3: Start with controlled repetitions, not to failure. DCU's own texts disagree on a few points, and Kadence shows the differences rather than hiding them.
points.4: During the growth spurt, keep an extra eye on pain at the knee and the heel.

growth.title: Growth spurt and biological age
growth.intro: Two riders in the same year group can be years apart in development. That affects both what they can take and how their results should be read.

points.1: The growth spurt typically starts around 10½–11 for girls and 12½–13 for boys, but for boys anything from 10½ to 16. It lasts 2–2½ years.
points.2: The skeleton is not fully developed until around age 20, and some boys grow until they are 20–22.
points.3: Technique and coordination can wobble during the spurt. Turn down jumps in load, and take pain at the knee (Osgood-Schlatter) and heel (Sever) seriously.
points.4: A rider born late in the year can be almost a year younger than a teammate in the same class. Record height in Kadence and judge development, not just results.

injury.title: Pain, illness and concussion
injury.intro: Kadence shows warnings, but the coach, the rider, the parents and in the end a doctor decide.

points.1: ATK's pain ladder is in Kadence's check-in. When pain changes the movement or stops training, the load comes down and a professional should look at it.
points.3: If concussion is suspected after a crash, the rider stops at once and sees a doctor. Danish guidance from 2024 allows light activity after 24–48 hours and a gradual return in six stages, where group rides and races come only when all symptoms are gone. The UCI requires juniors to wait at least two weeks after becoming symptom-free before racing again. The doctor decides.
points.4: On average it takes about 14 days to become symptom-free and 19 days to be fully back in sport. School comes back fully before full training.

sleepFood.title: Sleep, food and fluid
sleepFood.intro: Growing young people need more sleep and more food than one might think, and training only works when they get it.

points.1: Young people need 8–10 hours of sleep. Kadence's check-in shows sleep and warns when it is short again and again.
points.2: Regular meals and a snack before and after training. On rides over an hour, Team Danmark recommends 30–90 g of carbohydrate per hour.
points.3: Vitamin D, 10 µg a day from October to April. Girls need more iron after their first period, so with tiredness and frequent infections it is worth asking the doctor about iron.
points.4: Energy drinks with caffeine are not recommended for children and young people.
points.5: At camps and stage races with the same buffet every day, young people often eat less day by day. Keep an eye on it.

body.title: Body, weight and energy
body.intro: Cycling is a sport where talk about weight can do great harm. Kadence therefore has stricter defaults than most.

points.1: Team Danmark recommends, as a starting point, not weighing athletes under 18. Kadence goes further: no weight and no W/kg for riders under 19 unless the team turns it on.
points.2: Never comment on weight, body, food choices or portions, not even as a joke, and never talk about a rider's weight where others can hear. Every measurement needs a purpose and a conversation afterwards.
points.3: A Danish study from 2022 found signs of eating disorders in 23 % of female and 11 % of male elite athletes, and in even more at sub-elite level. Coaches' comments about weight loss were named as a trigger.
points.4: Signs of too little energy include a falling return from training, many injuries and infections, mood swings, and irregular or missing periods. The rider does not have to have lost weight. Refer to a doctor or sports dietitian, and do not calculate it yourself.
points.5: A missing period always goes to the doctor. Be open about the subject so riders dare to talk about it.

doping.title: Doping, medicine and supplements
doping.intro: The rider is always responsible for what they take, even when a supplement turns out to be contaminated. That makes good habits important early.

points.1: Strict liability means a positive test is the rider's responsibility, however the substance got into the body.
points.2: Under 18, ATK recommends no supplements other than vitamin D. Lists of performance supplements are written for adult elite athletes.
points.3: If supplements are used, only batch-tested products (for example Informed-Sport or the Cologne List), and keep the documentation.
points.4: Look medicine up with Anti Doping Danmark. Some asthma medicines are allowed up to a limit, while others, such as Bricanyl, need an exemption.
points.5: Since 10 February 2025 the UCI has banned CO-rebreathing equipment outside medical facilities.

wellbeing.title: Wellbeing and mental health
wellbeing.intro: Kadence's check-in helps you see how the riders are doing. It does not replace a conversation.

points.1: Team Danmark looks at mental health on four levels: the athlete, the training environment, the leadership and everyday life, each green, yellow or red. It is when someone stays in yellow or red for a long time that action is needed.
points.2: The parents' guide says: if a young person has struggled for about three weeks, have a talk within 14 days. Kadence shows when a rider has been in the yellow zone for too long.
points.3: In Team Danmark's 2024 wellbeing survey, 14 % had experienced boundary-crossing behaviour in the past year, most often belittling comments and comments about body and weight.
points.4: Help is available in the club, from DIF and from the municipality. For national-team environments, Team Danmark has EliteSupport.

school.title: School, exams and transitions
school.intro: Most U17 and U19 riders are in school, and school has to fit with the sport.

points.1: Put the school timetable and exams in the calendar, and lower the load and the expectations in exam periods.
points.2: The first months of a new upper-secondary school are hard. A couple of months with markedly less training can work wonders.
points.3: National-squad riders can apply for sporting approval for upper-secondary school with an extended programme and moved hand-ins and exams. The deadline is in January.
points.4: Agents make contact as early as U17 and U19. DCU offers independent advice on contracts.

heat.title: Heat and weather
heat.intro: Neither DCU nor Team Danmark has heat guidance for young riders. The advice here is Kadence's summary of general sources.

points.1: Sweat loss can reach 2 litres an hour. Drink steadily, but know that the body absorbs at most about 1–1.2 litres an hour. After the ride Team Danmark recommends 1.2–1.5 litres for every kilo lost.
points.2: Heavy sweating also costs salt, so think of salt on long, hot rides.
points.3: Move training to the morning or evening, and shorten the intervals on the hottest days.
points.4: The UCI's heat protocol for races judges the risk from both temperature and humidity.

parents.title: Working with the parents
parents.intro: Parents are the rider's most important support, and Kadence gives them a window in that the rider controls.

points.1: Parents see their child's training once the rider has confirmed the link, and check-ins only if the rider shares them.
points.2: The parents' guide from Team Danmark and Kolding Talent is on Kadence's parents' page. Point parents there.
points.3: There is one open conversation: comments on sessions and rides are read by coach, rider and parents.
points.4: For riders under 18, DIF recommends thinking the parents into the plan.
